abstract: The cerebral cortex is the major site of computation in the brain, and its recurrent wiring has motivated models in which repeated neuronal activation maintains information in stable attractor states. Large language models illustrate an alternative principle by transforming information layer by layer during each forward pass. A first step toward understanding what cortex and these models can teach us about each other is to establish whether feedforward dynamics can predominate in recurrent cortex. Here, we show that ongoing activity in the frontal cortex of awake mice is composed of parabolic neuronal avalanches in which activity progresses mainly through newly recruited neurons. Using two-photon calcium imaging in hundreds of simultaneously recorded layer II/III pyramidal neurons, we decomposed avalanche size into the number of participating neurons, mean activations per participant, and mean inferred spikes per activation. Avalanche size grew approximately quadratically with duration up to 0.5 s, primarily through recruitment of additional neurons. Participating neurons contributed close to one spike per avalanche on average. Newly recruited neurons also dominated the rise and fall of the average avalanche profile. An unbiased recruitment model, in which all neurons have the same selection probability, accounted for the predominance of new over repeat participation, showing that feedforward recruitment can dominate even when previously active neurons remain available for reactivation. Parabolic avalanches thus express predominantly feedforward dynamics within anatomically recurrent cortex. Cortical computation may therefore have more in common with feedforward processing in large language models than recurrent anatomy alone would suggest.
